text: {"answer": "The evidence is mixed, with several trials suggesting benefit but the best synthesis finding no clear advantage over standard calorie restriction. Supporting trials report that intermittent fasting combined with calorie restriction produced greater weight loss in obese women than the comparison diet [23334c40ad6b#1], and a high-protein intermittent-fasting diet produced weight loss in obese adults [c74e11d8769a#0]. A meta-analysis found intermittent energy restriction comparable to continuous restriction on weight loss and cardiometabolic outcomes [e5aee0e45fc5#0]. The contradicting evidence is substantial: a major Cochrane review of 22 trials with nearly 2,000 adults found intermittent fasting did not produce significantly more weight loss than standard diet advice [5a896703f2e3#0]. A Harvard review notes that research does not consistently show intermittent fasting is superior to continuous low calorie diets [44e3472ec92d#2], and a one-year trial of 100 obese individuals found it no more effective than daily restriction [44e3472ec92d#7]. One meta-analysis reported a modest advantage for fasting in body weight change [f5eeafdf6fc3#1]. Overall, it works about as well as continuous calorie reduction, but not clearly better.", "confidence": 62, "one_line": "Intermittent fasting produces weight loss, but major reviews find it generally no better than standard calorie restriction."}
